This page covers the specific U.S. occupation O*NET/SOC 51-8013.04, Hydroelectric Plant Technicians: monitoring and controlling activities associated with hydropower generation; operating plant equipment such as turbines, pumps, valves, gates, fans, electric control boards, and battery banks; monitoring equipment operation and performance and making necessary adjustments to ensure optimal performance; and performing equipment maintenance and repairs as needed. Official scope: Monitor and control activities associated with hydropower generation. Operate plant equipment, such as turbines, pumps, valves, gates, fans, electric control boards, and battery banks. Monitor equipment operation and performance and make necessary adjustments to ensure optimal performance. Perform equipment maintenance and repair as necessary. U.S. wage and employment data on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS employment projections for 2024—2034 as presented by O*NET; O*NET labels both datasets as aggregated data for Power Plant Operators. Exact occupational wage data for mainland China were not obtained and are recorded as a visible evidence gap. The jurisdictions and safety systems on the two sides are not interchangeable.

To assess your fit for work as a hydroelectric plant technician, first use public or simulated materials to complete a verifiable operating exercise. Set up a fictional generating-unit scenario, such as abnormal vibration and temperature, and write a step-by-step procedure covering shift handover and operating-parameter checks, equipment inspections and reading logs, anomaly identification and cause assessment, adjustment of valves and gates or starting and stopping auxiliary equipment according to procedures, isolation and tagging followed by maintenance or repair, and restoration of operation with reports to dispatchers and supervisors. Mark each safety and isolation checkpoint and possible problems: equipment failure, oil or water leaks, electrical hazards, work at height and noise exposure, and delayed anomaly reporting. Afterward, check whether power and water isolation, lockout/tagout, personal protection, and warnings are mandatory steps; whether electrical or pressure-equipment operations beyond your authority require stopping and escalation; and whether the basis for decisions and parameter readings form reviewable records. Assess yourself through an actual deliverable rather than an interest questionnaire alone.

Fit signals | Work activities for U.S. O*NET 51-8013.04 identify controlling machines and processes, identifying objects, actions, and events, inspecting equipment, structures, or materials, monitoring processes and surroundings, making decisions and solving problems, and obtaining information as the most important activities. Work-context responses include wearing common protective or safety equipment daily, 100%; face-to-face discussions daily, 88%; email daily, 86%; teamwork rated extremely important, 69%; constant contact with others, 54%; exposure to distracting or uncomfortable noise daily, 51%; very high responsibility for other workers' health and safety, 53%; consequences of error rated extremely serious, 36%; and exactness or accuracy rated very important, 56%. The most important skills include critical thinking, monitoring, reading comprehension, active listening, and speaking. Equipment maintenance, operation monitoring, operation and control, repairing, and troubleshooting rank highly among transferable skills. If you are willing to operate and inspect equipment according to procedures around rotating machinery and electrical systems, and take responsibility for safety and parameters, these daily demands may align more closely with your working style.

Caution signals | O*NET also reports for 51-8013.04: wearing common protective or safety equipment daily, 100%; very high responsibility for other workers' health and safety, 53%; exposure to hazardous equipment once a week or more, 42%; exposure to hazardous conditions once a week or more, 39%; exposure to high places once a month or more, 54%; exposure to contaminants once a month or more, 41%; working outdoors in all weather once a week or more, 43%; exposure to very hot or cold temperatures daily, 30%; and consequences of error rated extremely serious, 36%. This occupation involves rotating machinery, energized equipment, high-pressure water systems, and plant environments. A single failure in isolation or lockout/tagout, unauthorized operation of energized or pressure equipment, misread parameter, or unreported anomaly may cause injury, equipment damage, or a power-supply incident. This page therefore addresses isolation and lockout/tagout, personal protection and hazardous work, parameter monitoring and anomaly reporting, and operating-authority limits separately. The U.S. occupation itself is not marked Bright Outlook. The O*NET page shows a projected decline of -11% for 2024—2034, approximately 2,500 annual openings, and about 31,600 people employed in 2024 for the related aggregate category, Power Plant Operators. These are aggregated Power Plant Operators data, not the precise size of this occupation. If rotating machinery and electrical risks, outdoor and noisy environments, or shift duty would be difficult for you, treat them as real costs requiring careful consideration.

Responsibility assessment | Genuine fit depends on whether you can accomplish three things within the same shift: carry out operations thoroughly, including handover parameter checks, equipment inspections, anomaly identification and adjustments, and maintenance or repairs as needed, producing reviewable operating and maintenance records; maintain safety and isolation through power and water isolation, lockout/tagout, personal protection and warnings, and hazardous-work permits according to procedures and organizational requirements; and accept defined job responsibilities, taking responsibility for your own operations, parameter judgments, and records, while stopping and escalating high-voltage electrical or pressure-equipment work beyond your authority under the applicable system. Test this through a verifiable experience, such as producing a step-by-step operating procedure and operating log, or practicing the identification and handling of common equipment anomalies, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire.

The daily work of hydroelectric plant technicians can be divided into three strands: (1) operations and monitoring—checking parameters at handover, inspecting equipment, recording readings, and making adjustments in accordance with specifications to maintain stable generating-unit operation; (2) faults and operations—identifying and addressing equipment malfunctions, starting, adjusting, or stopping units, and operating valves, gates, and auxiliary equipment; (3) maintenance and safety—performing preventive and corrective maintenance, isolation and lockout/tagout, containment or cleanup to prevent pollution, and equipment-status reporting and recordkeeping. All three share the same safety and parameter requirements but produce different outcomes: operations concern unit condition, fault handling and operations concern equipment actions, and maintenance and safety concern equipment availability and risk control.

O*NET 51-8013.04, Hydroelectric Plant Technicians: monitor and control activities associated with hydropower generation; operate turbines, pumps, valves, gates, fans, electric control boards, battery banks, and other equipment; monitor equipment operation and performance and make necessary adjustments; and perform maintenance and repairs as needed. Core tasks include monitoring equipment operation and performance, identifying and addressing malfunctions, starting, adjusting, or stopping generating units, inspecting equipment and determining repair needs, performing containment or cleanup to prevent pollution, and reporting equipment status. Job Zone Three: medium preparation needed.

items.title: Education, training, and qualifications: what are the real entry requirements?

paragraphs: Qualification boundary one | Education, training records, special-operation certificates, job authorization, and work permits are different statuses. Meeting education and training requirements does not mean obtaining a special-operation certificate, and obtaining a certificate does not authorize a particular instance of high-voltage electrical or pressure-equipment work.

Qualification boundary two | In mainland China, power-production roles involving electrical and similar work are governed by workplace safety regulations and organizational systems. These requirements are jurisdiction-sensitive and must follow current regulations and competent-authority requirements.

Qualification boundary three | In the U.S. O*NET survey, 34% report a postsecondary nondegree certificate and 34% an associate's degree. The Job Zone group description is not a uniform training duration for this occupation and does not establish China's legal entry requirements.

Qualification boundary four | Preparation items on this page are directions for searching and checking, not any organization's official qualification list. Organizational announcements and competent-authority requirements take precedence if they differ. This page provides no conclusions about individual ability or background, hiring likelihood, or pay promises.

Recruitment sample note | This page cites no counts or pay figures from specific job postings. Hydroelectric plant technician roles are commonly entered through generation groups, plant or grid organizations, and industrial captive power plants. Public-channel samples are unlikely to represent the entire market; organization type, generating units, and region substantially affect staffing scale.

Checking recommendation | When reading recruitment information, record publication date, location, organization and generating-unit type, role category (operations, repairs, or operation and maintenance), shifts and duty arrangements, certification and work-permit requirements, safety training, and pay structure. These reveal actual conditions better than job titles. These are editorial checking recommendations, not quotations from current vacancies.

entries.answer: According to O*NET 51-8013.04, this occupation monitors and controls activities associated with hydropower generation; operates turbines, pumps, valves, gates, fans, electric control boards, battery banks, and other equipment; monitors equipment operation and performance and makes necessary adjustments; and performs maintenance and repairs as needed. Typical tasks include monitoring equipment operation and performance, identifying and addressing malfunctions, starting, adjusting, or stopping generating units, inspecting equipment and determining repair needs, performing containment or cleanup to prevent pollution, and reporting equipment status.
entries.question: What do hydroelectric plant technicians do?

entries.answer: Hydroelectric production managers handle operating plans and staffing and budget decisions; power plant operators work across multiple forms of generation; industrial machinery mechanics focus on general machinery installation and repair; wind turbine service technicians work on turbines and at height; and water and wastewater treatment plant operators work on water-treatment systems. Equipment, qualifications, and safety procedures differ, so titles cannot be treated as interchangeable.

subject.name: Hydroelectric Plant Technicians
subject.summary: Hydroelectric plant technicians correspond to the specific U.S. occupation O*NET/SOC 51-8013.04, Hydroelectric Plant Technicians: they monitor and control activities associated with hydropower generation; operate turbines, pumps, valves, gates, fans, electric control boards, battery banks, and other equipment; monitor equipment operation and performance and make necessary adjustments; and perform maintenance and repairs as needed. Official scope: Monitor and control activities associated with hydropower generation. Operate plant equipment, such as turbines, pumps, valves, gates, fans, electric control boards, and battery banks. Monitor equipment operation and performance and make necessary adjustments to ensure optimal performance. Perform equipment maintenance and repair as necessary. Core tasks include monitoring equipment operation and performance, identifying and addressing equipment malfunctions, starting, adjusting, or stopping generating units, inspecting equipment and determining repair needs, performing containment or cleanup to prevent pollution, and reporting equipment status. U.S. wage and employment data on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS employment projections for 2024—2034 as presented by O*NET; O*NET labels both datasets as aggregated data for Power Plant Operators. Exact occupational wage data for mainland China were not obtained and are recorded as a visible evidence gap. Qualification and workplace safety requirements in China are marked separately.
